title: Contractual discretion
summary: Contractual discretion is a party’s power to make a choice affecting performance, such as whether a result is satisfactory, how much to order, or how strongly to promote a product. The question is what limits govern that choice.
notes:
A contract can leave room for judgment without leaving a party free of all obligation. In Mattei, the buyer could evaluate proposed leases but had to be genuinely dissatisfied rather than use the condition to escape an unwanted bargain. In Structural Polymer, uncertain requirements were constrained by good faith and the agreed purchasing arrangement. In Wood, the exclusive agency and revenue-sharing structure implied reasonable efforts even without an express sentence saying so.

Later cases ask how discretion is exercised after formation. Dalton examines a testing service’s obligation to consider evidence within its promised review process. Bloor examines efforts to market a brand where royalties depended on sales. Market Street addresses the use of a contractual procedure and possible exploitation of the other party’s oversight. Ng Giap cautions that a broad good-faith obligation cannot simply be assumed across jurisdictions or used to rewrite express rights.

To analyze discretion, identify the exact choice, the person entitled to make it, the contractual purpose, and the relevant standard. A reasonableness standard asks whether the choice meets an external benchmark. A subjective good-faith standard asks whether the stated judgment is genuine within the agreed undertaking. Express terms and governing law determine which applies. A judge’s discretion over procedure or remedies is a different issue.
